**Video:** [Lec 65 — Introduction to Generative Models](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hgZ3HOMkrx0)

## Learning goals

- Contrast **generative** models ($p(x)$ or $p(x,y)$) with **discriminative** models ($p(y\mid x)$ or $f(x)\to y$).
- List what “generate” means: sample new $x\sim\hat p$.
- Preview major families: explicit density (VAE-like), implicit (GAN), and modern likelihood models (brief).

## Before this clicks

A classifier only needs a decision boundary or $p(y\mid x)$. A generative model aims at the **data distribution** itself: where probability mass lives in $x$-space (images, text tokens, audio). If you can sample from that model, you can create new examples that look like the training set.

---

## Main ideas

### 1. Discriminative vs generative

| Type | Models | Typical use |
|------|--------|-------------|
| Discriminative | $p(y\mid x)$ or score $f(x)$ | Classification / regression |
| Generative | $p(x)$ or $p(x,y)$ | Sampling, density, imputation, …

Generative $\Rightarrow$ discriminative is possible in principle via Bayes rule when $p(x\mid y)$ and $p(y)$ are modeled; the converse does not give you samples of $x$.

### 2. Why generative models?

- synthesize data (images, text)
- fill missing parts / denoise
- anomaly scoring via low $p(x)$
- representation learning through latent $z$

### 3. Modeling styles (map)

1. **Explicit normalized density** — write $p_\theta(x)$ and maximize likelihood (or ELBO when exact likelihood is hard): classical mixtures, autoregressive models, VAEs (variational bound).
2. **Implicit models** — define a sampler $x=G_\theta(z)$, $z\sim p(z)$, without a closed-form density: **GANs**.
3. **Energy / score / diffusion** families (course may only glance): learn how to move noise toward data.

### 4. Latent-variable intuition

Many deep generative models use

$$
z\sim p(z),\qquad x\sim p_\theta(x\mid z).
$$

Marginal $p_\theta(x)=\int p_\theta(x\mid z)p(z)\,dz$ is often intractable — hence VAEs (bound) or GANs (avoid computing it).

### 5. Evaluation (beginner caution)

- Likelihood on held-out data (when available)
- Sample quality / diversity (FID-style metrics in vision)
- Downstream usefulness of latents

Good samples $\neq$ perfect density; good likelihood $\neq$ always pretty samples.

---

## Worked mini-example

Discriminative: given face pixels $x$, predict age $y$. Generative: learn $p(x)$ over face images and draw new faces $\tilde x\sim\hat p$. A conditional generative model $p(x\mid y)$ could draw “faces that look age-$y$.” Same pixels, different question.

---

## Common confusions

| Confusion | Clarification |
|-----------|---------------|
| Generative = always deep nets | Mixtures and PCA-Gaussian models are generative too. |
| Classifier samples new $x$ | Discriminative models generally **cannot**. |
| One family wins forever | Tradeoffs: likelihood vs sample quality vs training stability. |

## Self-check questions

1. What distribution does a generative model primarily target?
2. Can a pure discriminative $p(y\mid x)$ model draw new $x$?
3. Write the latent-variable generative story $z\to x$.
4. Name one explicit and one implicit deep generative family.
5. Give one application beyond “pretty samples.”

*(Short answers are in `self-check-answers.qmd`.)*
